directions: The appellants are sentenced to suﬀ er rigorous imprisonment for 7 years.

issue.issue_text: whether, the conviction under Section 302 of IPC would be tenable or not.

facts: The incident arose from a dispute over a buffalo belonging to the complainant's party spoiling a structure built by the accused.
The accused formed an unlawful assembly and assaulted the complainant's party, resulting in one death.
There was a cross-case registered against the complainant party, and members of the accused party also sustained injuries.
The defense argued that the complainant party initiated the assault, leading to a free fight.
law: To sustain a conviction under Section 302 (murder) read with Section 149 (unlawful assembly) of the IPC, the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the common object of the unlawful assembly was to cause death.
If the defense provides a probable explanation for injuries on the accused, it can create doubt about the prosecution's case.

Section 304 Part-II of the IPC applies to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, where an act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without the intention to cause death.
application: The Court found there was no clarity as to whether the common object of the unlawful assembly was specifically to cause the death of the deceased.
The prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the assembly had a shared intention to commit murder.
The existence of a cross-case and injuries on the accused, coupled with the defense's claim of a free fight, created doubt about the prosecution's version of events.
Given these doubts, the Court determined that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the doubt regarding the charge of murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction under Section 302 of the IPC was not sustainable. It held that the prosecution failed to prove the intention to cause death, and therefore altered the conviction to the lesser offense under Section 304 Part-II of the IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder).

issue.issue_text: Whether the courts below were justiﬁ ed in convicting and sentencing the appellants for the oﬀ ences punishable u/s. 302/149, s.326/149, s.324/149, s.323/149, s.147 and s.148 IPC.

facts: The incident originated from a dispute where a buffalo belonging to the complainant's party spoiled a structure ('taparia') built by the accused.
Following this, the appellants and others formed an unlawful assembly and assaulted the complainant and his family members with deadly weapons.
The assault resulted in the death of one person from the complainant's party and injuries to others.
Members of the accused party also sustained injuries, and a cross-case was registered against the complainant's party, suggesting a free fight occurred.
law: The central legal question involves determining the 'common object' of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

The Court must distinguish between the intention to cause death (required for a murder conviction under Section 302 IPC) and the knowledge that an act is likely to cause death (sufficient for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-II IPC).
The principle of 'benefit of doubt' is applied when the prosecution fails to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court cast doubt on the prosecution's case for several reasons: the non-explanation of injuries sustained by the accused, the existence of a cross-case which indicated a 'free fight' rather than a one-sided attack, and the fact that the witnesses were 'interested witnesses'.

The Court noted that the entire incident arose from a trivial matter (the buffalo spoiling the taparia), which made it unclear if the common object of the unlawful assembly was actually to cause someone's death.
The Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the unlawful assembly shared a common intention to kill the deceased.
While the appellants were part of the unlawful assembly, their actions were deemed to fall short of murder, as the specific intent to kill was not established.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the doubt regarding the charge of murder. It held that the conviction under Section 302 (murder) was not sustainable. Instead, the Court found that the case fell under Section 304 Part-II (culpable homicide not amounting to murder). Consequently, it altered the conviction and reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment, thereby finding the lower courts' judgments to be only partly justified.

arguments.issue_text: whether, the conviction under Section 302 of IPC would be tenable or not.
appellant_arguments: The witnesses who denied the presence of injuries on the accused are lying on a material point, making their evidence unreliable.
respondent_arguments: Both the trial court and the High Court have concurrently found that the prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
Since the appellants were part of an unlawful assembly, it was not necessary for the prosecution to attribute specific individual roles.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the courts below were justiﬁ ed in convicting and sentencing the appellants for the oﬀ ences punishable u/s. 302/149, s.326/149, s.324/149, s.323/149, s.147 and s.148 IPC.
appellant_arguments: The witnesses who denied the presence of injuries on the accused are lying on a material point, making their evidence unreliable.
respondent_arguments: Both the trial court and the High Court have concurrently found that the prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
As the appellants were part of an unlawful assembly, it was not necessary for the prosecution to attribute specific roles to each individual.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code is not sustainable when the prosecution fails to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that an unlawful assembly had the intention to cause death; in such circumstances, the offense may be classified under Part-II of Section 304 of the IPC.
obiter: The punishment prescribed by Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code is vicarious in nature and does not always proceed on the basis that the offense has been actually committed by every member of the unlawful assembly.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the unlawful assembly had a specific intention to cause the death of the deceased. The non-explanation of injuries on the accused, coupled with a plausible defense version of a free fight, created sufficient doubt to negate the intent required for a murder conviction under Section 302 IPC. Therefore, the conviction is altered to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-II IPC, as the appellants are entitled to the benefit of the doubt regarding the charge of murder.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that non-explanation of injuries on the accused by the prosecution can be fatal to its case, particularly when: "(1) that the prosecution has suppressed the genesis and the origin of the occurrence and has thus not presented the true version; (2) that the witnesses who have denied the presence of the injuries on the person of the accused are lying on a most material point and therefore their evidence is unreliable; (3) that in case there is a defence version which explains the injuries on the person of the accused it is rendered probable so as to throw doubt on the prosecution case.”
The distinction between the requisite intent for murder under Section 302 IPC and the knowledge that an act is likely to cause death for culpable homicide under Section 304 Part-II IPC.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants did not secure a full acquittal because the court still found them guilty of being members of an unlawful assembly that caused a death, establishing vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC. While the specific intent for murder was not proven, the court determined that the facts supported a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-II IPC, for which the prosecution's evidence was sufficient.
why_respondent_won: The respondent partially succeeded because the court affirmed that the appellants were part of an unlawful assembly responsible for the death, even if the specific intent for murder was not proven. The court found that "the case would fall under Part-II of Section 304 of IPC," thereby upholding a conviction for a serious offense and accepting the principle of vicarious liability, which meant it was not necessary to attribute specific individual roles for the fatal injury.
